title: Which Range Holds the Point?

concept.title: Binary search for the last range that starts at or before the point, then check its end
body: A timetable has `n` closed ranges (both the start and the end belong to the range). They are sorted and disjoint. For each query point, which range holds it? Print the **number of the range** (counting from 1) or `0` if no range holds the point. For the ranges `(1, 3) (5, 9) (12, 12)` the points `0 2 4 9 12 13` give `0 1 0 2 3 0`.

Scanning all the ranges for every query is O(n * q), 2.5 billion steps in the worst case. But the ranges are sorted and do not overlap, so only **one** range can hold the point: the **last range whose start is at most the point**. Find it with a **binary search** on the starts, and then check whether the point is also at most the end of this range. If no start is at most the point, or the point is beyond that range's end, the answer is 0.

Each query takes O(log n), so the whole work is O((n + q) log n). The key fact is that the sorted starts split the line into pieces and every point belongs to exactly one candidate range. In C++ the same search is `upper_bound`, and in Java it is written by hand.

statement: `n` closed ranges are given in increasing order; they do not overlap. For each of `q` points print the number of the range (counting from 1) that contains it, or 0 if no range contains the point.
inputFormat: The first line has `n` and `q`: the number of ranges and the number of questions.
Each of the next `n` lines has two numbers `start` and `end`: a closed range (both ends belong to it). The ranges are given in increasing order and do not overlap.
The last line has `q` numbers: the points to look up.
outputFormat: Print `q` numbers on one line, separated by spaces.
hints: Only the last range that starts at or before the point can hold it.
Find it with a binary search on the starts.
Then check that the point is not beyond its end.

explanation: For each point a binary search finds the last range whose start is at most the point; the point is inside that range exactly when it is not beyond its end, and the answer is the number of that range or 0.
solution.complexity: Time O((n + q) log n), space O(n).

code.python:
import sys
input = sys.stdin.readline

from bisect import bisect_right

n, q = map(int, input().split())
ranges = [list(map(int, input().split())) for _ in range(n)]
points = list(map(int, input().split()))

starts = [r0[0] for r0 in ranges]
out = []
for p in points:
    k = bisect_right(starts, p) - 1
    if k >= 0 and p <= ranges[k][1]:
        out.append(k + 1)
    else:
        out.append(0)
print(*out)
